question: Which animal leathers are permissible, and does tanning make an animal's skin pure?
asked: What types of animal leather are allowed? If I tan an animal's leather, does it purify it and make it permissible to use?
answer:
So this is a fiqh question, obviously, that deals with animal leather. So I'll give you the brief answer and I'll give the detailed answer. The brief answer is that tanning is a type of complete transformation called istihala that makes the najis into tahir, that makes that which is impure into that which is pure. And therefore, the point of tanning the skin is to transform that which is najis into tahir. And from a technical perspective, there should be no difference between any animal skin. Once it is transformed, anything that was najis becomes tahir. And this would include pig leather, nonetheless.

I advise you to avoid pig skin, because the majority position is that it should be avoided, and because we really don't want to get involved with that animal. **And other than pig, all other hides and all other leather, inshallah, is permissible.** This is the fatwa that I am giving you.

Now the detailed response, the longer answer. The skins of animals: obviously a dead animal, an animal that is found dead, a mayta, that you have not killed, that is najis, and you cannot use it. You cannot do anything with it in that state. It is a dead animal. We are talking about tanning the skin. We're talking about taking the skin, and there are methods to tan it in our times; chemically it is done. In the good old days, they would add ammonia and they would put it in the sun, and they would do a lot of things, and they would do a chemical process. And then the final product would now be the tanned leather that would then be used for garments. It would be used for utensils. It would be used for putting on things.

So again, leather has been used since the beginning of time, and Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala mentions in the Qur'an, "wa min aswafiha wa awbariha": you're going to benefit from animal skin, animal leather and animal fur. This is explicit in the Qur'an, that it is allowed for us.

However, the controversy exists over what animal skins are allowed. And this controversy has manifested amongst the four madhhabs and beyond. Obviously, as usual, I always give the caveat: this is the short answer. There are actually 10 opinions on this, no exaggeration, 10 opinions on this issue. We are not going to go over every single one of them. Very briefly, I'll just mention four or five of them so that you understand what the controversy is.

The first opinion I'll mention is the most restrictive position, which is found within the Hanbali school, certain segments of the Hanbali school, and certain segments of the Maliki school. And these scholars said that the only leather that is allowed to use is the leather of the animal that has been slaughtered properly for the dhabiha, the dhabiha animal that has been slaughtered properly. That is the only animal that you can then take. So obviously animals that are not allowed to eat automatically get kicked out the window, but even animals that are allowed to eat, if they have not been slaughtered, some of these scholars say you cannot use them at all. So if a goat dies naturally, if an owner of a camel comes one day and he finds a dead camel in his flock of camels, according to this opinion, that's it, nothing. You cannot touch it; it is completely gone. This is the most restrictive of the opinions out there.

The next opinion, the second one that I'm going to mention, is the more common position amongst the Hanbalis and Malikis, and it is the position of Ibn Taymiyyah and of Ibn Qudama and most of my own teachers as well, which is that all animals that are permissible to eat may be utilized, their skins may be utilized, even if they have not been slaughtered. Therefore, going back to our example: camels, goats, sheep, cows, whether you slaughter them or not doesn't matter. You can take the skin, you can tan it, and the tanned skin is permissible, okay?

So the difference between the first and the second category is, the first category says you must slaughter the animal, and only if the animal is slaughtered is the skin then permitted. This position, as far as I understand, has pretty much been abandoned in the modern world. It is almost impossible to implement, and frankly, the evidences do not support it. The other opinion is the more common opinion, and it is the general position of the modern Hanbali school and the Maliki school and, as I say, Ibn Taymiyyah and Ibn Qudama. And that is that all animals that may be eaten, their skin may be tanned and utilized, regardless of whether you sacrifice the animal or the animal was found dead.

And the evidence for this is the hadith of Ibn Abbas radiyallahu 'anhu, that once the Prophet passed by a dead sheep, and it had been gifted to Maymuna, his wife. And of course it died naturally. So the Prophet said to his family, "Why don't you benefit from the skin? Why don't you benefit from the skin?" So they said, "O Messenger of Allah, it's a mayta; it's dead. How can we benefit?" So our Prophet ﷺ said, "Innama haruma akluha": what is forbidden is to eat the animal. This hadith is in Bukhari and Muslim. This hadith is super, super explicit.

And that's why the position that is known amongst the Hanbalis and the Malikis, which is the fatwa that is given, is that it's very clear: even if the animal is dead, you can take the skin off of it, peel the skin off of it, and then do the tanning process and then benefit from it. Because our Prophet said (the hadith is in Muslim, from Ibn Abbas as well): if the skin has been tanned, it becomes pure. So tanning of the skin of the animal makes it pure.

So this is the second opinion. And this is the majority position, and there's no question that it is a correct opinion. You do not have to slaughter the animal.

Okay, now we get to an even broader one. We're going from the narrowest to the broader: the third opinion. And the third opinion is that of Imam al-Shafi'i, and the Shafi'i madhhab is on this position, and many of the Hanafis are on this position as well. And that is that all animal skin is halal except for two animals: pig skin and dogs. This is the majority Shafi'i position. And he used the hadith that any skin that has been tanned becomes tahir. He said the hadith is very clear: any skin. He didn't just say lamb skin or sheep skin or goat skin or camel skin or cow skin. He said any animal skin.

Therefore Imam Shafi'i said, we make no exceptions, but he did; he made two exceptions. He said, we'll make an exception for a pig, because the pig is explicitly mentioned in the Qur'an as being najis, something that is filthy. So he said, the pig we'll make an exception for. And then he said, we'll make qiyas upon the dog, because the saliva of the dog is najis, and so the dog we'll put in a similar category as the pig. Not that anybody uses dog skin anyway, so we don't have to worry that much about that. But the point is, this is the Shafi'i position.

And Ibn Abdul Barr, the famous Maliki scholar, says, "Wa 'alayhi jumhur al-fuqaha' min ahl al-nadhar wa al-athar bil-Hijaz wa al-'Iraq wa al-Sham": this is the position of the majority of the scholars of the Hijaz and of Iraq and of Syria. This is the default position of the majority of the scholars, he said. And this would imply that, for example, in our times crocodile skin is allowed, right? Because crocodile skin is used. Now, again, I'm not talking about the ethical issues. That's another issue altogether. I'm not saying to ignore it. I'm simply saying I'm speaking as a faqih, what needs to be said from fiqh. I'm not speaking as an ethicist about whether this should be done to these animals or not. That's a whole totally different issue altogether.

So according to this position, pig hide, pig leather, would not be allowed, but any other leather (nobody uses dog leather), anything else would be permitted other than that.

Now the fourth position is that of Imam Abu Hanifa and some of the Hanafi scholars, and they said that we will allow even, theoretically, dog; we're simply only going to restrict it to pig. So Abu Hanifa said all animal hide is allowed except for pig. The only difference between him and Imam Shafi'i: Imam Shafi'i said pig and dog, and Imam Abu Hanifa said only pig.

The fifth opinion, and the final one we'll quote, is that of the student of Abu Hanifa, Imam Abu Yusuf, and also the founder of the fifth madhhab (you know, there are actually more than four madhhabs, so they say the fifth madhhab is called the Zahiri madhhab), Dawud al-Zahiri. Dawud al-Zahiri and Abu Yusuf made no exceptions. They said, once the Prophet ﷺ said any animal skin that is tanned becomes pure, who are we to make any conditions? So they said all animal skins that are tanned become pure, including pig leather.

And from a purely technical, from a purely theoretical perspective, I am sympathetic to this position, because it is based upon sound reality of the paradigm. What I mean by this: I gave a whole talk, it's on the Q&A if you look at it, on chemical change and gelatin. Listen to that talk and then link it to this one. I spoke a little bit about that some months ago (I think it was a year ago) when I spoke about gelatin and the issue of chemical transformation, and the position that a chemical transformation, or what is called istihala, changes najas into tahir. And this is the correct opinion. If you follow this opinion, then tanning is an example of a chemical transformation. If you say that tanning is chemical transformation, then no matter what the product was in the beginning, the final product will be tahir.

And therefore Imam Abu Yusuf and Dawud al-Zahiri and those who gave this fatwa are being consistent, and those who bring in pig skin are using an emotional argument that I love as well. So from a purely theoretical perspective, I understand Imam Abu Yusuf and Dawud al-Zahiri, and they are consistent, and I like that. But the fatwa that I give is that of Imam Abu Hanifa, which is: use any skin other than pig skin, okay? That's what I said in the beginning.

And if somebody were to insist and use the pig skin, they're following great 'ulama and whatnot. But why go down this route? Let's just try to avoid at least the one animal that Allah has said should be avoided. And really, there's just no need to go there. Nonetheless, if somebody has a particular item from beforehand that is coming from this animal and it has been tanned, there is precedent to use it, even though I would never personally advise anybody to go buy this, just to get out of the khilaf, and just to realize that the vast majority of the ummah were uncomfortable in this regard, even if from a purely theoretical perspective tanning does make the najis into tahir.

That having been said, there is another prohibition that you should be aware of (or I should say it's not haram, but it is makruh), and that is to use the skins of predatory beasts for decoration: lions and leopards and tigers. You know, we don't do this as Muslims. We don't have their skins. Why? Our Prophet ﷺ said (the hadith is in Tirmidhi, narrated by Abu Malih from his father) that the Nabi ﷺ "naha 'an julud al-siba' an tuftarash", rawahu al-Tirmidhi: the Prophet ﷺ forbade that the skins of predatory animals be laid out.

You know, in those days kings and arrogant people and the multi-millionaires would have the skins of lions and the skins of tigers and the skins of leopards, and this would be a token of pride. And they would make saddles on their horses and camels made out of leopard, for example, just to show the people that they have the power, and the flaunting. So this hadith says the Prophet ﷺ forbade that the predatory skins be rolled out and used as carpets.

Imam al-Tirmidhi narrates this hadith, and then Imam al-Tirmidhi says: some of the people of knowledge from the Sahaba and those after them disliked that the skins of predators, even if they are tanned, be used. And this is the position of Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak and Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh. And they were even more strict that those skins should not be worn or be used as prayer rugs, okay? So they disliked that you even have them, and they hated, nearly the level of haram basically, that you wear them. So it's one thing to display them; they said that's makruh, should not be done.

And of course, I mean, in every issue there's khilaf, but this is the Hanbali position. And there is a hadith here. I mean, stick with the hadith as much as possible: our Prophet ﷺ is saying that they should not be used as furush. And the least that can be said is that it is makruh, because there's a level of arrogance that is done. When you have those animal skins, you're trying to be boastful and whatnot. So it is best to avoid those skins, not because they are najis, but because the issue comes of showing off.

And therefore, to conclude this question, the fatwa that I'm giving is basically a modified Shafi'i fatwa (because nobody uses dog skin) and the Hanafi position, which is that the skins of all animals other than pig are permissible. And I don't encourage pig skin whatsoever, but if somebody were to insist and have it, there is precedent, and it does make theoretical sense. Nonetheless, we should avoid pig skin, simply because Allah 'azza wa jal has called pig in the Qur'an something that is filthy, and so we should try to avoid it as much as possible. And in the end, Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala knows best.
